name: datatype-channel
intent: Bind each channel to exactly one message type - the channel's identity is the type contract - so that a sender selects the channel that matches the data it holds and a receiver, knowing the channel it consumed from, knows what the payload is and how to process it without inspecting it.
problem: Several kinds of data travel over the same messaging infrastructure, and each kind has its own contract, decoder, consumers and delivery policy. If they share one channel (or one undifferentiated topic), every receiver must inspect the payload or a type header to find out what it got; the type contract becomes implicit, stringly typed and easy to break, and any change to one type's format threatens every consumer of the channel.
context: Asynchronous messaging between components that are deployed, scaled and versioned independently, where the set of message types is small, closed and known at design time - orders, invoices, readings, domain events. Applies both to middleware channels (queues, topics, subscriptions, consumer groups) and to in-process hand-off (Go channels, Rust mpsc, C# Channel<T>, coroutines Channel<E>, Akka ActorRef[T], AsyncStream), because in both cases the receiver must know the type before it decides how to decode and route.
benefits: The contract becomes explicit and static: one channel carries one type, so decoder, validation and domain mapping are chosen when the subscription is wired instead of being derived from the payload at runtime.

Producers cannot accidentally hand a consumer something it cannot process - the typed primitive refuses it at compile time, the destination name misroutes it at publish time, not deep inside the consumer.

Per-type policy is possible: retention, ordering, retry, dead-letter destination, schema and version, access control and throttling can differ per type because the channel is the unit of configuration.
Independent scaling: partition counts, consumer groups and competing consumers are tuned per message type instead of for the union of all traffic on a shared channel.
Parallel evolution: adding a message type adds a channel and a consumer without editing central dispatch logic or renegotiating one omnibus schema.
Observability per contract: depth, age and consumer lag per type show which message flow is in trouble, which a single multiplexed channel hides.
tradeoffs: Channel sprawl: every type consumes broker resources - queues, bindings, subscriptions, ACL entries, dashboards, on-call runbooks - and a growing domain keeps multiplying destinations.

Schema evolution multiplies as well: a new incompatible contract version either needs a new channel (version in the name) or in-message versioning, which partially weakens the clean type-to-channel binding.

The naming scheme and topology become governed artifacts: a typo or an inconsistent convention silently creates a second channel nothing consumes, and the failure mode is data quietly piling up instead of an exception.
Low-volume types pay full price: a channel with three messages a day needs the same setup, monitoring and alerting as a busy one, and many sparse channels make operations noisy.
Polymorphic or genuinely variable payloads fit badly: widening the type (Channel<Base>) reintroduces dispatch in the consumer, while enumerating every subtype explodes the destination count.

In-process typed channels do not remove the classification problem: the sender must still decide which type a value is at the call site, so a mis-wrapped value is a producer-side design risk rather than something the compiler can catch.
Cross-cutting concerns (correlation, tracing, security context) must be attached to every channel instead of once on a shared pipeline, which pushes work into per-type configuration.
In distributed brokers, channel-per-type can create hot spots: a high-volume type monopolizes broker resources while others sit idle, requiring careful partition and consumer-group planning.

Routing by type at publish time introduces a static dependency: producers must hard-code or look up the channel name for each type, creating a bootstrap problem when a new type is introduced in a polyglot system.

participants.responsibility: Owns a value, classifies it and selects the channel that carries that message type; it never writes a type discriminator into the payload.
The typed channel itself - a queue, topic, subscription, named destination or in-process typed primitive - whose identity equals exactly one message type; nothing else is allowed on it.

The shared convention (naming scheme, constant table, schema-registry subject, exchange/binding topology) that binds type to destination, so producers and consumers agree without inspecting a message.
Subscribes to exactly the channels it serves; it derives the message type and codec from the channel identity and therefore never has to ask 'what is this?'.
The per-channel decoder, validator and error path: it materializes the type at the boundary and routes undecodable payloads to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel.

use_cases: Command channels in an order-to-cash backend: place-order, cancel-order and issue-invoice each have their own queue, so the payment handler can never receive an order-placement command by mistake.
Telemetry pipelines where temperature, pressure and status readings travel on separate topics with different retention, sampling and alarming policies.
Enterprise integration between an ERP and a CRM: exchange-rate feeds, master-data updates and transactional documents on separate channels with different guarantees, ACLs and dead-letter paths.
In-process pipelines in Go, Rust, Kotlin or C#: chan Order, mpsc::channel::<Order>() or Channel<Order> wiring the stages, so each stage's signature documents exactly what it consumes.
Multi-tenant device gateways: one destination per measurement type, so a stalled consumer of one type cannot hold up the others.
Regulatory and audit streams (sanctions-screening results, payment confirmations) that need longer retention and stricter access than ordinary business events.

Hybrid durability routing: payment authorizations, order creation and customer-visible notifications routed to durable Kafka topics; internal price calculations, cache invalidation and metrics fan-out routed to in-process Go channels for sub-millisecond latency.

Kafka multi-tenant subject naming: using TopicNameStrategy where each topic maps to one message type and schema subject, enabling independent schema evolution per type with compatibility checking scoped to that topic.

Event-sourcing aggregates: each aggregate type (Account, Order, Shipment) publishes its events to a dedicated stream, so projectors can subscribe to exactly the events they need without filtering a generic event bus.

Confluent Schema Registry with the default TopicNameStrategy: the schema subject is derived from the topic name, so the registry's compatibility checking enforces one record type per topic - the datatype channel encoded in the registry itself.

NATS deployments: one message type per dot-delimited subject organized as app.region.service.entity.action, so consumers subscribe narrowly to a single type or capture a type family with wildcard subscriptions.

WSO2 Integrator (MI) implements the EIP Datatype Channel directly: an upstream router dispatches each message to a channel dedicated to its data type, so every downstream mediation flow receives uniformly typed messages.
avoid_when: Exactly one kind of message flows between the parties and no second type is plausible: a single well-named channel or in-process queue is simpler; the pattern is a policy for sets of types.

The set of types is open or unknown at design time (plugins, arbitrary user payloads): put a type or format indicator inside the message and route on content, because channels cannot be named for types you cannot enumerate.
The payload is a self-describing document and the receiver decides by content: one document channel plus content-based routing is the simpler fit.

Producer and consumer live in one process and already share a typed API: a direct call, a callback or a single queue is enough; the pattern pays off at middleware boundaries and with independently deployed consumers.
The channel must carry a stable contract and only the payload version changes: use in-message versioning or a format indicator rather than creating one channel per schema version.
anti_patterns: Type tag on a shared channel: everything goes to one queue and every consumer switches on a type field - exactly the dispatch the pattern removes, and the reason all consumers must be redeployed for each new type.
Channel per entity instance (queue-per-order-number, topic-per-device-id): unbounded destination creation no broker or operator can manage; the channel identity must be the type, not the data.
Version channels (orders-v1, orders-v2, orders-v3) used instead of message versioning, so the topology grows with every release and consumers chase channels.
Naming by convention with no single source of truth: the type-to-channel map lives in string literals across repositories and diverges at the first refactor, producing orphan channels.
Typed channel only at the edges: an in-process Channel<Order> fed by a shared 'any' channel, so the type dispatch simply moves to the transport boundary and returns.
Channels created without consumers, alarms or retention policy: destinations fill silently until the broker's limits are reached and the first sign of trouble is a production incident.
Hard-coded topic/queue names in producer code: changing a topic name requires redeploying every producer; use a naming registry or constant table.
Schema ID not embedded in serialized messages: consumers cannot fetch the correct schema for decoding after schema evolution.
design_principles: Explicit contract over implicit convention: the channel's identity states the message contract, so no receiver has to guess.
Single responsibility per channel: one type, one decoder, one consumer group, one policy.
Static binding where the language allows it (chan T, Channel<T>, ActorRef[T], AsyncStream<Element>), validation at the boundary where it does not.
Information hiding: the receiver learns the type from the transport decision it subscribed to, not from the payload's contents.
Open for extension, closed for modification: a new message type is a new channel plus a new consumer, never an edit to a central dispatcher.
Design for operations: every channel is a monitored, governed resource with its own error and retention policy.
Schema registry per topic: embed a schema ID in each message so consumers can fetch and apply the correct schema version independently of the channel.
Idempotent consumers everywhere: since at-least-once delivery is the norm in distributed brokers, design every message handler to tolerate (and deduplicate) duplicate deliveries.
best_practices: Define the type-to-channel mapping once - a constants map, an enum with destination names, a schema-registry subject scheme - and let both producers and consumers derive destinations from it.
Bind per-channel policy explicitly: retention, ordering guarantee, dead-letter destination, retry and backoff, ACL and consumer group per message type.
Validate and decode at the channel boundary with one decoder per channel, and route undecodable messages to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel.
Keep channel names stable, human-meaningful and version-free (domain type, not schema version or environment) and evolve contracts by message versioning instead of renaming channels.
Alarm per channel on queue depth, age of the oldest message and consumer lag; a channel nobody watches is a silent data sink.
Prefer the language's typed primitive when one exists (chan<- Order, Channel<Order>, ActorRef[Order]) so that misuse is a compile or type error rather than a runtime incident.
Keep the type set small and closed; when the types cannot be enumerated, switch to a format indicator plus content-based routing.

Use a schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, Redpanda Schema Registry, AWS Glue) to manage schema versions per topic, configure compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) per subject, and embed schema IDs in serialized messages so consumers can fetch the correct schema on deserialization.

Apply the hybrid durability routing rule: route must-not-lose messages (payments, orders, regulatory events) to durable brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ with publisher confirms) and route recomputable, latency-sensitive messages (cache invalidation, metrics, internal state updates) to in-process typed channels.

Design idempotent message handlers: store processed event IDs with a unique constraint, use domain IDs as natural idempotency keys, or write to an inbox table in the same transaction as business changes.

Set explicit prefetch and back-pressure: in RabbitMQ, configure prefetch count per consumer; in Kafka, partition by the ordering key relevant to the message type (e.g., order_id for order events) to preserve per-key ordering.

Implement retry with exponential back-off and a dead-letter topology: requeue with a retry count header, after N retries route to a dead-letter queue; avoid infinite immediate requeue which creates hot loops.

When combining multiple event types on one broker topic is unavoidable (e.g., for per-key ordering across types), use RecordNameStrategy or TopicRecordNameStrategy in Confluent Schema Registry to maintain schema-per-record-type isolation, and configure ksqlDB schema constraints appropriately.
Monitor per-channel consumer lag and set alerting thresholds: a channel with zero lag but zero throughput indicates a misconfigured consumer group, not a healthy system.
sources: Hohpe, G. & Woolf, B., Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions, Addison-Wesley (2003) - Datatype Channel (Messaging Channels chapter).
